144-001.r: Atmosphere is heated mostly indirectly: Earth absorbs short-wave solar energy and gives out long-wave radiation, absorbed by carbon dioxide and greenhouse gases; A and R true, R explains A.

144-002.r: Temperature falls with height because the atmosphere is heated upward from Earth's surface and upper air is less dense; upper air is not moister.

144-003.r: Fresh snow reflects most sunlight → albedo 75-95%; Earth's average albedo 30%; sand desert 20-30%; paddy cropland 3-15%.

144-004.r: Tropical cyclones weaken away from the sea: their energy is latent heat from condensing ocean moisture, which falls inland; both true, 2 explains 1.

144-005.r: Albedo → reflecting power of a surface; ice has a high albedo, forests and green plains a low one.

144-006.r: Bigger oceans have smaller annual temperature range, so the Atlantic's range exceeds the Pacific's; Northern Hemisphere's annual range exceeds the Southern's.

144-007.r: January isotherms bend north over oceans and south over continents; Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift are warm, not cold, currents, so statement 2 is wrong.

144-008.r: January, Northern Hemisphere: isotherms bend equatorward over land and poleward over oceans, because oceans are then warmer than land; both true, II explains I.

144-009.r: Highest temperatures are recorded near 20°N, not at the Equator. True: water vapour varies a lot in lower air; frigid zones lie between polar circles and poles.

144-011.r: Clear nights are cooler due to radiation: Earth's heat escapes freely to space, while clouds trap it and send it back on cloudy nights.

144-012.r: Infrared waves are largely absorbed by water vapour concentrated in the lower atmosphere; short-wave solar energy passes through the atmosphere easily.

144-013.r: Urban heat island → city hotter than nearby rural areas, due to concrete, asphalt, little vegetation, less evapotranspiration, and heat from vehicles and industry.

145-001.r: Only some cyclones develop an eye (true). Jet streams blow in both hemispheres, about 8-15 km up, west to east; the eye being 10°C cooler is false.

145-002.r: In a cyclone, surface winds spiral inward to a low-pressure centre and air descends at the centre; A and R true, R explains A.

145-003.r: Cyclone figure: area D (cold front) gets heavy, short, torrential rain with thunderstorms; ahead of the warm front (A) clouds bring steady precipitation.

145-004.r: Tornadoes → small, very powerful funnel-shaped storms born from thunderstorms, most frequent in the USA; exam keys link them with the Caribbean Sea.
145-004.c: The book calls tornadoes tropical cyclones; they are short-lived funnel storms born from thunderstorms, most common over the USA plains, not true tropical cyclones.

145-006.r: Tornado Alley → plains of mid-USA (Mississippi plains): Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, Mississippi and Missouri valleys, where polar cold air meets warm humid air.

145-007.r: Tornado intensity → Fujita (Fujita-Pearson) scale, the F-scale, named after Ted Fujita.
145-007.t: Don't confuse with the Saffir-Simpson scale, which rates hurricanes.

145-008.r: Typhoons → mature tropical cyclones of the China Sea, northern hemisphere, between 100°-180°E.

145-009.r: Tropical cyclone names: Australia → Willy-Willy (north and north-west Australia); China → Typhoon; India → Cyclone; USA → Hurricane.

145-011.r: Willy-Willy → Australia; Hurricane → USA; Typhoon → China; Baguio → Philippines.

145-013.r: Willy-Willies → Australia; Taifu → Japan; Baguio → Philippines; Hurricanes → USA.

145-014.r: Hurricane damage → Saffir-Simpson Scale: rates wind speed on 1-5 to estimate property damage and coastal flooding.

145-015.r: Sudden fall of mercury in a barometer → stormy weather (a violent storm is coming).

145-016.r: Cyclone Nargis hit Myanmar, not India; cyclones Aila, Thane and Neelam affected India.

145-017.r: No tropical cyclones form in the South Atlantic and south-east Pacific tropics because sea surface temperatures there are low.

145-018.r: Global warming (IPCC) → cyclones, storms and hurricanes all grow more frequent and severe; also glacier melt, sea-level rise, worse floods and droughts.

145-019.r: 2019 storms: Dorian → Bahamas; Hagibis → Japan; Lekima → China; Mitag → Jeju, South Korea.

146-001.r: Air moisture falls with latitude (tropics 2.6%, down to 0.2% at high latitudes) because warmer air holds more water vapour; A and R true, R explains A.

146-002.r: Humid summer heat → muggy weather. Absolute humidity = weight of water vapour per unit volume of air.

146-003.r: Humidity → presence of moisture (water vapour) in the air.

146-004.r: No dew on cloudy nights: clouds reflect Earth's radiation back, so surfaces do not cool below dew point. Dew → condensation on surfaces colder than dew point.

147-001.r: Sub-polar low-pressure belt lies at 60°-65° latitude in both hemispheres; low-pressure areas are steadier over oceans; both true, but R does not explain A.

147-002.r: Horse latitudes → about 30°-35° N and S: the subtropical high-pressure belts, where rising equatorial air, deflected poleward, sinks.

147-004.r: Air pressure is lowest in summer: pressure is inversely related to temperature. Pressure also falls with altitude.

148-001.r: Clouds → condensation of water vapour into tiny water droplets or ice crystals.

148-002.r: Cumulonimbus → dense clouds giving heavy, short-lived rain, hail and thunderstorms.

148-003.r: Highest clouds among options → cirrostratus, formed above about 18000 feet.

148-004.r: Thunderclouds develop from condensation, high temperature and humidity, and strong vertical (upward) winds; orography is not among the key's causes.

148-005.r: Thunder → sound of lightning: lightning heats the air in its channel, which expands supersonically as a shockwave; none of the listed causes is right.

148-006.r: Cirrus cloud thinning and stratospheric sulphate aerosol injection → climate-engineering ideas for reducing global warming.

148-007.r: No dew on cloudy nights: clouds reflect Earth's radiation back, keeping the surface warm. Dew needs clear sky, calm air, high humidity, long cool nights.

149-001.r: Coriolis force → increases with wind speed; maximum at the poles, absent at the Equator; deflects winds right in the north, left in the south.

149-002.r: Tropics: trade winds (east to west) make western parts of oceans warmer; temperate zone: westerlies make eastern parts warmer. Both true.
149-002.h: Wind pushes warm water to the side it blows towards.

149-003.r: Coriolis effect deflects winds right (clockwise) in the Northern and left (anti-clockwise) in the Southern Hemisphere; A and R true. The reversed assertion is false.

149-005.r: Winds deflect left in the Southern Hemisphere due to the Coriolis force (Ferrel's law: right in the north, left in the south).

149-006.r: Southern Hemisphere westerlies are stronger and steadier because it has less landmass; the Coriolis force is not higher there.

149-007.r: Coriolis force balanced by pressure-gradient force → geostrophic winds, blowing parallel to isobars aloft. Roaring forties etc. → Southern Hemisphere westerlies.

149-009.r: Roaring forties, furious fifties, shrieking sixties → Southern Hemisphere westerlies, named for their intensity.
149-009.h: Forties roar, fifties rage, sixties shriek: wilder towards the South Pole.

149-010.r: Roaring Forties → strong, constant westerlies of the Southern Hemisphere (40-60 degrees south), north-west to east, with overcast skies, rain, raw weather; not in the north.

149-013.r: Winds deflect left in the Southern Hemisphere because of the Coriolis force, which arises from Earth's rotation.

149-014.r: The Mediterranean lies in the subtropical high-pressure belt: trade winds blow there in summer and westerlies (anti-trades) in winter.
149-014.c: The book gives no single answer (*): both trade winds and westerlies blow from these latitudes.

149-015.r: Seasonal reversal of winds → monsoon climate: winds blow sea to land in summer and land to sea in winter.

149-016.r: Chinook ('snow-eater') → warm wind down the eastern Rockies in winter and early spring; quickly raises winter temperature, melts snow, frees pasture.

150-001.r: Foehn → Alps (Switzerland); Simoom → Arabia and Kurdistan deserts; Santa Ana → southern California; Zonda → Argentina (east Andes).

150-003.r: Wrong: Bora → cold dry wind of the eastern Adriatic coast (affects northern Italy), not Poland. Foehn → Alps; Khamsin → Egypt.
150-003.c: The Mistral blows down the Rhône valley in France, not the Rhine; unless 'Rhine' is a misprint for Rhône, (c) is also a wrong pair alongside (b).

150-004.r: Wrong: Blizzard (strong snowstorm) → South Pole, Siberia, Canada etc., not Chile. Correct: Chinook → USA; Sirocco → Sicily; Norwesters → India.

150-005.r: Blood rain → Italy: the Sirocco from the Sahara carries red sand, which falls with raindrops.

150-006.r: Wrong: Sirocco is not France's; it carries Saharan dust from Libya to Malta, Italy, Croatia, Greece etc. Correct: Bora → Italy; Blizzard → Canada.

150-007.r: Chinook ('snow eater') → warm dry wind down the eastern Rockies (Colorado to British Columbia); raises winter temperature, melts snow, frees pasture for cattle.

150-008.r: Wrong: Mistral → France and Spain, not Australia. Correct: Santa Ana → California; Haboob → Sudan; Yamo → Japan.

150-009.r: Wrong: Shamal → hot dry dusty wind of Iraq, Iran and Arabian Peninsula (June-August), not Austria. Correct: Leveche → Spain; Brickfielder → Australia; Black roller → North America.

150-010.r: Harmattan → cool, dry north-east/east wind blowing west across the Sahara; called 'Doctor Wind' for its invigorating dryness.

151-001.r: Selva → broad-leaf evergreen equatorial forests of the Amazon basin (Brazil); high temperature and rainfall above 200 cm all year.

151-002.r: Selvas → Brazil's equatorial rainforests (true). Terra Roxa → fertile dark-purple soil from limestone and dolomite in south and south-east Brazil, not 'dark black'.

151-003.r: Altitude 400 m, maximum 28-31°C and minimum 20-21°C all year, rain every month → tropical rain forest.

151-004.r: Largest share of world forest area → temperate coniferous forests, mainly in high latitudes.

151-005.r: Bhutan's constitution requires 60% of its area under forest; forest cover is now (2025) 70.13%.

151-006.r: Evergreen rainforests → near the Equator, hot with rain all year and no dry season: Amazon basin (Brazil), Congo Basin etc.

151-010.r: Taiga (coniferous or boreal forest) → temperate region; northernmost temperate biome across North America and Eurasia; short summers.

151-011.r: Largest and densest forest → Amazon basin rainforest (Brazil); the basin covers 60% of South America.

151-012.r: Forest share of land (World Bank 2023): Japan 68.4% > Indonesia 47.7% > India 24.5% > China 24.0%.

151-013.r: Coniferous forests (50°-60°N, between tundra and deciduous forest) → Canada, Scandinavia, Finland; not Amazonia, which has tropical evergreen forest.

151-014.r: Coniferous forests → mainly in temperate regions.

151-015.r: Dense, hot, humid forests in Africa → Ivory Coast, on the Gulf of Guinea coast.

151-016.r: Cleared tropical rainforest does not give lasting farmland, temperate forest does (A false); rainforest primary productivity is very high, 2200 g/m²/year (R true).

151-017.r: Tropical rainforest regenerates slowly after clearing because its soil is poor in nutrients.

151-018.r: Rainforest soil is poor in nutrients (Statement I false); heat and moisture decompose dead matter quickly (Statement II true).
151-018.t: Don't confuse rich vegetation with rich soil.

151-019.r: Cedar → Canada; Douglas Fir → Mexico; Mahogany → Honduras; Teak → Myanmar.

151-020.r: Monsoon forest → teak, sal; Equatorial → mahogany, rosewood; Mediterranean → plum, olive; Coniferous → pine, spruce.

151-021.r: Softwood and wood pulp → Canada led when asked; FAO 2025 yearbook: USA now tops wood pulp (2023), then Brazil and China.

151-022.r: Largest fuelwood producer → India (FAO 2025 yearbook, data 2023), then China, then Brazil.

151-023.r: Dalbergia → rosewood genus (Sheesham, kingwood, tulipwood); trees of the Americas, Africa, Madagascar and tropical South Asia.

151-024.r: Desert plants cut water loss with hard waxy leaves, tiny leaves and thorns instead of leaves; also long roots and thick bark.

151-025.r: Maquis → Mediterranean coast; Fynbos → South Africa; Chaparral → California; Matorral → Chile.

151-026.r: Epiphytes → Equatorial; Acacia → Sahara; Baobab → Savanna; Cedars → Mediterranean.

151-027.r: Fast leaf-litter decay, bare soil surface, climbers and epiphytes reaching the canopy → tropical rain forest.

151-028.r: Highest deforestation → tropical forest zone; forests covered about 4.1 billion ha (31%) of land in 2020, largest share tropical (SOFO 2024).

151-029.r: Mahua and Teak → deciduous; Jackfruit → evergreen (about 25 m tall, yields latex). So only two are deciduous.

151-030.r: World's largest tropical peatland → Congo Basin; its peat swamp forests store about 29 billion tonnes of carbon, about three years of global emissions.

151-031.r: Forests control the hydrological cycle: canopy intercepts rain, high transpiration, deep roots lift soil water, rich soils hold water and recharge groundwater.

152-001.r: Seasonal change in day and night length comes from Earth's revolution around the Sun on a tilted axis; without the tilt, days and nights would be equal everywhere.
152-001.c: The book keys '2 and 4'; the cause is revolution with a tilted axis (statement 4). The elliptical shape of the orbit (statement 2) is not the reason.

152-002.r: Continental interiors have a high annual temperature range due to the land-water thermal difference: land heats and cools fast, water slowly.

152-003.r: Main factor deciding the climate of an area → latitude; major climate belts follow latitudes.

152-004.r: Largest share of Earth's surface → arid regions, about one-third.

152-005.r: Equatorial belt → high heat and rain all year; high temperature and humidity give convectional rain, mostly after noon; A and R true, R explains A.

152-007.r: Asia → has all climate types (tropical, temperate, cold), as it stretches from the equatorial region to the North Pole.

152-008.r: Ethiopia → not equatorial climate; Congo, Gabon and Zaire (DR Congo) lie on the Equator.

152-009.r: Warm dry summers, mild wet winters and evergreen oak trees → Mediterranean region.

152-010.r: Tropical savannah → a definite dry and wet season, high temperatures all year, rainfall 500-2000 mm.

152-011.r: Equatorial regions suit plants (evergreen forests), not humans (humid, disease-prone); low annual temperature range is true but not the reason.

152-012.r: Mediterranean climate → west sides of continents: Rome, Los Angeles (south California), central Chile, Cape Town, south Australia; not New York (east coast USA).

152-013.r: Mediterranean climate: winter rain and dry summer under offshore (terrestrial) trade winds; both true, but the real cause is the seasonal shift of pressure and wind belts.

152-014.r: Mediterranean climate → rain in winter, dry summers; at winter solstice the pressure belts shift south. Both true; climate comes from seasonal belt shifts.

152-015.r: Extreme climate, scanty rain, nomadic herders → Central Asian Steppe.

152-016.r: Correct: Equatorial zone → convectional rain with thunder around noon. Mediterranean → winter rain; monsoon → rain from monsoon winds; deserts → negligible rain.

152-017.r: Map area 1 (California) → Mediterranean climate: hot dry summer, mild moist winter, seasonal reversal of winds.

152-018.r: Norway → West European climate with ample rain all year, including winter; China-type climate has a relatively dry winter.

152-019.r: Wet winter, dry summer → Italy (Mediterranean). Sudan → tropical, desert parts very dry; Iran → hot, dry; northern Chile → hot, dry desert.

152-020.r: California → Mediterranean; West Australia → Hot Desert; Bangladesh → Tropical Monsoon; Siberia → Cold Temperate.

152-021.r: Equatorial → Congo; Mediterranean → California; Monsoon → Bangladesh; Savannah → Sudan.
